finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice with no authentication or ownership check (IDOR / broken access control). The sibling /my/invoice route does enforce customer == g.user['id'], which shows the check was intended here too.
finding.source: Any HTTP client supplies inv_id in the URL path. It needs no authentication and no relationship to the invoice's customer.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field and any billing data.

trace.note: Route /invoice/<inv_id> registered with no auth decorator and no before_request hook in the file
INVOICES.get(inv_id) fetches the record by the attacker-supplied key, with no ownership comparison
The full invoice is serialized and returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: There is no g.user check in this handler. By contrast, get_my_invoice at invoices.py:16 compares inv['customer'] to g.user['id']. No app-level before_request or auth middleware exists in this file; g.user is set by code outside the file, and even where it is set, this handler never reads it. If invoice IDs are sequential or guessable, the whole invoice table can be enumerated.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no auth decorator or before_request hook, fetches INVOICES.get(inv_id) and returns jsonify(inv) without any g.user ownership check, unlike invoices.py:16 in the sibling route.

verdict_facts.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no decorator, auth check or ownership comparison and returns jsonify(inv) for any key, while the sibling at invoices.py:16 does check g.user['id'], and this directory has no other files or middleware that could block it.
